Every morning at a quarter past seven a man came in for bread. He came from the night shift at a dry cleaner’s in the Baixa and he smelled of steam and hot cloth, like a shirt just off the iron, and he always had a joke. They were terrible jokes. She did not laugh at them, for six months, on principle. He did not stop. Every morning, one joke and one loaf.

“And one morning in winter he came in and said nothing at all. He paid for his bread and stood there, and she saw he had been crying, because his mother was in the hospital. And she did not know what to say. So she told him a joke. It was a terrible joke. She had been saving it for six months in case she ever needed it. And he laughed so hard he had to sit down on the floor of the bakery, among the flour sacks, and she laughed too, and she could not stop, and the owner came out from the back to see who was dying.
“That was how it began. Not with his jokes. With hers. He never knew that. He thought he had won her with his jokes. He had won her by needing one.”
My eyes burned. Nothing came. Nothing had come since the beach. I had not cried at my mother’s funeral, or at my wife’s. I had told jokes.
“You were not a bad husband,” she said. “You were a frightened one. Those are different things. She knew the difference. She knew it better than you did.”

She stood up. In seven months I had never seen her stand. She came across the room and stood in front of me, and put her hand on my face, and I smelled orange blossom, and bread, and the river, and, for the first time, underneath, nothing. No fear at all. Only her.
“Go down the stairs, Vasco,” she said. “Not the steps. The stairs.”

I did not see her go. I closed my eyes to keep the smell a moment longer, and when I opened them, the room was dark, and the curtains were shut, and the furniture was under its white sheets, and I was sitting on a bare mattress in an empty room, and I was awake.
40. At six in the morning, before the taxi came, I opened the drawer by the bed.
It was not her birthday. That was the rule, and I broke it. I cut the bag open for the fourth and last time, and put my face inside, and breathed.
Warm bread. The almond soap from the box with the blue bird. Her hair.
And that was all.

The fear was gone. The coin and the onion, which I had smelled in that pillowcase three years running, which I had smelled on her every day of her last seventeen years, was not there. I breathed in again and again, with my face pressed into the cotton, and it was not there.
It had never been in the pillowcase. It had never been hers. It had been mine, and I had been smelling it on everything I loved, and last night I had set it down.
What was left was only her. I had not smelled only her since 2004.

I sat on the bed with my face in the pillowcase until the taxi sounded its horn in the street. Then I folded it, with the corners turned in like an envelope, and put it back in the drawer, and did not seal it, and went down the stairs.

41. They opened my head on the eleventh of June and took the growth out, and with it, as she had promised, the two thin nerves that had brought the world in through my nose all my life, and I woke up in a room that smelled of nothing at all.
42. I will tell you what it is like, since I am one of the few people who can tell you both sides.

It is like a city with the sound turned off. Everything is where it was. The trams still run up the hill to Graça, the washing still hangs across the alleys in Alfama, the river is still there at the bottom of every street. But it has gone flat, like a photograph of itself. I walk through it the way you walk through a museum.

Food is the worst. Nobody warns you. Most of what we call taste is smell, it turns out, and without it the tongue on its own can tell you only a few plain things: sweet, salt, sour, bitter. A pastel de nata is a warm, sweet, soft thing. A grilled sardine is a hot, salty, oily thing. Coffee is bitter water. I eat because I must.

And the jokes have gone. That surprised me most. I had not known how many of my jokes came through my nose, how much of my whole life was that: coming into a room and smelling it, and saying something clever about what I smelled, so that nobody would look at me. Now I come into a room and there is nothing to say. I am a comedian with no material. I stand there. People look at me.
I have let them.
43. In August I went back to the Estrela.

The manager did not want me. What use, he said, kindly, is a night laundryman without a nose? I told him that the machines do not know the difference. São Pedro said something to him that I did not hear, and he gave me my job back.

So I wash the sheets. The chute speaks at two in the morning, and the bags come down, and I untie them, and I do not put my face to them, because there is nothing there for me to read. I load the machines. I fold. I press. The businessman from Porto has his heart attacks on Tuesdays, I suppose. The sisters are still sisters. The man in 517 may still be crying about Marta. I will never know.

I think of the washerwomen of Caneças, carrying the city’s sheets home on their donkeys, knowing everything and saying nothing. What the cloth tells you, the water keeps. For twenty years I broke that rule every night. Now I could not break it if I tried. I wash what the city cannot say, and I do not ask.

I emptied the cage in September. I did not burn the sheets. I washed them, all six sets, one set at a time, on a long hot cycle, and dried them and ironed them and folded them with the corners turned in like envelopes, and I put them back into the hotel’s own linen, onto the shelves, among the others. They are on the beds of the Estrela now, somewhere, clean. Guests sleep in them and do not know. That seemed the right place for them. Not a grave. A bed.

At three o’clock I go up to the desk. The radio plays fado, very low. São Pedro pours the ginjinha into the chocolate cups. It tastes of sweet and of nothing. He asks me, every night, “Well?” And I say, every night, “I have no idea,” and it is the truest thing I have said at that desk in twenty years.
He has started to laugh at it.
THE SAINT OF LOST THINGS

Santo António, Saint Anthony, was born in Lisbon at the end of the 1100s, and though he died far away in Italy, and most of the world calls him Anthony of Padua, Lisbon has never let him go. He is the city’s own saint. He is known for two things: he helps you find what you have lost, and he helps you find someone to love.

Every year, on the night of the twelfth of June, the eve of his feast, the whole of Lisbon goes out into the street. The old quarters, Alfama and Graça and Mouraria [moh-ra-REE-a] and the rest, hang paper garlands and coloured lanterns across every alley, and set up tables and grills outside every door. These street parties are called arraiais [a-ra-YAISH]. The smoke of grilled sardines, eaten on thick bread that soaks up the oil, rises over the whole city, so that for one night Lisbon smells of one thing from end to end. Each neighbourhood sends a costumed parade, the marchas [MAR-shash], dancing down the great avenue, and the city stays up singing until the sun comes over the river. On that same day, the city marries its Santo António couples.

And on that night, people give each other a manjerico [man-zhe-REE-koo]. It is a small pot of bushy, sweet basil, round as a ball, with a paper carnation stuck in it and a little paper flag carrying a four-line love verse, a quadra [KWAA-dra]. In the old days a young man gave one to the girl he loved, and she kept it on her windowsill all year, until he brought her the next.

There is one rule about the manjerico, and everybody in Lisbon knows it. You must never put your nose to it. The old people say that if you sniff it, it will die. Instead, you brush the palm of your hand lightly over the top of it, and then you lift your hand to your face and smell your own palm.
The scent is carried to you on your own skin. That is the only way it is allowed to come.
Take this little pot of basil and its paper carnation too; don’t smell it, or it will die.
Smell your hand; it is more true.
Santo António finds what is lost. He does not always give it back. Sometimes he only shows you where it went.
44. On Saturday the thirteenth of June, 2026, Santo António’s day, I crossed the river.

It was twenty-two years to the day. The city was still hoarse from the night before, and the paper garlands were still up across the alleys, and the grills were being lit again outside the doors in Alfama. I walked through the smoke of a thousand sardines and smelled nothing. I watched the people breathing it in, their faces opening as they did, and I knew exactly what it was they were smelling, and it was as far from me as the moon.

I took the tram to Belém. I bought a ticket for the ferry, and it cost one euro and some cents, and the man in the booth did not look up, and it was the simplest thing in the world. I had not done it in twenty-two years.

I stood at the rail. The wind came up off the water into my face, and I closed my eyes the way he had, and I felt it, cold and wet and clean, and I could not smell it, and that did not matter as much as I had feared.

At Trafaria I walked down onto the sand. It was hot. There were families under umbrellas, and children at the edge of the water with buckets, and a restaurant behind the beach grilling sardines for the saint. I walked down to the place. I knew the place. I have always known it. Twenty metres from where the umbrella had been, where the sand goes dark and wet, where the river is getting ready to become the sea.

I stood there at the edge of the water and I said it out loud. Not loudly. Nobody on that beach heard me, or if they heard me, they did not look up. I said it to the river, because the river was the only one who had been there who had not already heard it.
“I was asleep,” I said.
The river did what rivers do. It came in, and it went out.

Then I sat down on the sand, and I stayed there all afternoon, until the families packed up their umbrellas and went home to their parties, with my arms round my knees and my eyes open, watching the children at the edge of the water. I did not lie down. I did not close my eyes once. It was the least I could do, and twenty-two years too late, and I did it anyway.
45. When the ferry brought me back across to Belém, it was evening, and São Pedro was standing on the quay.

He was in his grey day suit. I had not told him where I was going. He had not needed telling; he keeps the doors of the whole city, and he knows the dates. He was holding something in both hands, carefully, the way he holds the key to a good room.
It was a manjerico. A small round pot of basil, bright green, with a red paper carnation stuck in the top, and a little paper flag with a verse on it that I did not read.
“For the saint,” he said. “It is his day. Somebody should give you one.”
I took it. It weighed almost nothing. I held it the way you hold a thing that is alive and might die of the wrong kind of love.

I did not put my nose to it. I know the rule. I brushed the palm of my right hand over the top of it, lightly, the way my mother taught me, the way Inês did every June on our windowsill. I felt the little leaves spring back against my skin. Then I lifted my hand to my face, and closed my eyes, and breathed in.
Nothing.

My own palm, and nothing. Not the basil. Not the river, or the sardines, or the salt of the evening. Not Inês’s hands, which had done this on our windowsill every June, and which I had always, always smelled on mine afterwards. Nothing at all.
And my body, which had carried the truth for twenty-two years and had finally, on that beach, been allowed to set it down, did the only thing it had left.

I stood on the quay at Belém with a pot of basil in one hand and my face in the other, and I wept for my son, and for my wife, and for the smell of his head on the morning he was born, and for all of it, for the first time since the river, with the whole city singing for its saint behind me, and São Pedro standing beside me with his hand on my back, not saying a word.
I could not smell any of it. But my face was wet, and the wet ran down to the corner of my mouth, and I tasted it.
Salt. That much they cannot take from you.

Alcobaça [al-koo-BAA-sa] — A town north of Lisbon whose great monastery holds the tombs of Pedro and Inês de Castro.
Alfama [al-FAA-ma] — Lisbon’s oldest quarter, a maze of steep alleys on the hill below the castle.
Alto de São João [AAL-too de sow zhoo-OW] — Portuguese, Saint
John’s Heights. One of Lisbon’s large cemeteries, on a hill in the east of the city.
arraiais [a-ra-YAISH] — Portuguese, street parties. The neighbourhood festivals of June, with lanterns, music and grilled sardines.
bacalhau [ba-ka-LYOW] — Portuguese, salt cod. Cod dried and salted stiff, the national food of Portugal.
Bairro Alto [BAI-roo AAL-too] — Portuguese, the High Quarter. A hilltop district of Lisbon known for its bars and fado houses.
Baixa [BAI-sha] — Portuguese, the low town. Lisbon’s flat centre by the river, rebuilt in straight streets after 1755.
Belém [be-LAYNG] — A riverside district of west Lisbon; the name means Bethlehem.
Cais das Colunas [KAISH dash koo-LOO-nash] — Portuguese, the
Quay of the Columns. Marble steps between two stone columns leading from Lisbon’s great square down into the river.
Cais do Sodré [KAISH doo so-DREH] — Portuguese, Sodré’s Quay.
The old riverside docks district of Lisbon, once the sailors’
quarter.
calçada [kal-SAA-da] — Portuguese, pavement. Lisbon’s hand-laid pavements of small black and white stones, beautiful and slippery in the rain.
calceteiros [kal-se-TAY-roosh] — Portuguese, pavers. The craftsmen who set the calçada stone by stone.
Camões, Luís de [loo-EESH de ka-MOYNSH] — Portugal’s greatest poet, who published the national epic in 1572.
Caneças [ka-NAY-sash] — A village on the hills north of Lisbon, famous for its springs and its washerwomen.
Coimbra [KWEEM-bra] — Portugal’s old university city on the river
Mondego, where Inês de Castro was killed.
Desejado, o [oo de-ze-ZHAA-doo] — Portuguese, the Desired One.
The name given to King Sebastião, whose birth the country had prayed for.
Diário Popular [DYAA-ryoo poo-poo-LAAR] — Portuguese, the
People’s Daily. A Lisbon newspaper that began the Santo
António weddings in 1958.
Dom [dom] — Portuguese, lord. The title given to Portuguese kings and nobles.
Dona [DOH-na] — Portuguese, lady. A respectful way to address a woman.
Estrela [esh-TRAY-la] — Portuguese, star. The name of the hotel where Vasco works.
fado [FAA-doo] — Portuguese, fate. Lisbon’s mournful folk song of loss and the sea, sung by one voice with two guitars.
Fonte das Lágrimas [FON-t dash LAA-gree-mash] — Portuguese, the Fountain of Tears. A spring in a garden in Coimbra, said to have risen from the tears of Inês de Castro.
ginjinha [zheen-ZHEE-nya] — Portuguese, little sour cherry. A sweet, dark liqueur made from sour cherries, drunk from tiny cups.
Graça [GRAA-sa] — Portuguese, grace. A high neighbourhood of
Lisbon where Vasco lives.
Inês [ee-NAYSH] — Portuguese form of Agnes. Vasco’s wife.
Inês de Castro [ee-NAYSH de KASH-troo] — A noblewoman from
Galicia, beloved of Prince Pedro, killed at Coimbra in 1355.
lavadeiras [la-va-DAY-rash] — Portuguese, washerwomen. The village women who once washed Lisbon’s laundry by hand in the streams.
Lisboetas [leezh-BWAY-tash] — Portuguese, people of Lisbon. The people who live in Lisbon.
luto [LOO-too] — Portuguese, mourning. The custom of wearing black after a death, sometimes for years.
manjerico [man-zhe-REE-koo] — Portuguese, bush basil. A pot of basil with a paper carnation and a love verse, given on Santo
António’s night.
marchas [MAR-shash] — Portuguese, marches. The costumed parades each neighbourhood sends dancing through Lisbon on
Santo António’s eve.
Marta [MAAR-ta] — The name the man in room 517 cries in his sleep.
Mondego [mon-DAY-goo] — The river that runs through Coimbra.
Mouraria [moh-ra-REE-a] — Portuguese, the Moorish quarter. An old neighbourhood of Lisbon where the Moors lived after the city was taken.
mouras encantadas [MOH-rash en-kan-TAA-dash] — Portuguese, enchanted Moorish girls. Spirit maidens of legend, bound by a spell to springs and wells.
Ofiusa [o-fee-OO-za] — Greek, land of serpents. The half-serpent queen of the legend of Lisbon’s founding.
pastel de nata [pash-TEL de NAA-ta] — Portuguese, cream pastry.
Lisbon’s custard tart, eaten warm with cinnamon.
porteiro da noite [poor-TAY-roo da NOY-t] — Portuguese, porter of the night. The hotel worker who keeps the front desk and the keys overnight.
quadra [KWAA-dra] — Portuguese, set of four. The traditional four-line Portuguese folk verse.
Rua Augusta [ROO-a ow-GOOSH-ta] — Portuguese, August Street.
The long street of shops leading down to Lisbon’s great square.
Rua da Graça [ROO-a da GRAA-sa] — Portuguese, Graça Street.
The main street of Graça, where Inês sold bread.
Rui [HOO-ee] — The night porter’s brother, lost with the cod fleet.
Santo António [SAN-too an-TO-nyoo] — Saint Anthony, born in
Lisbon: finder of lost things, patron of lovers. His feast is 13
June.
São João [sow zhoo-OW] — Saint John. On his eve, 23 June, the mouras encantadas appear.
São Pedro [sow PAY-droo] — Saint Peter, who holds the keys of
Heaven. Vasco’s name for the night porter.
saudade [sow-DAA-d] — Portuguese, longing. Loving someone in the shape of the space they left.
sebastianismo [se-bash-tya-NEEZH-moo] — Portuguese,
Sebastianism. The belief that the lost king would return; a hope that refuses a death.
Sebastião, Dom [dom se-bash-TYOW] — King of Portugal, lost in battle in Morocco in 1578, aged twenty-four.
Senhor [se-NYOR] — Portuguese, sir. The Portuguese form of
Mister.
Tomás [too-MAASH] — Portuguese form of Thomas. Vasco’s son.
Trafaria [tra-fa-REE-a] — A fishing town on the south bank, where the river meets the sea.
Vasco [VAASH-koo] — A Portuguese name, carried by the navigator
Vasco da Gama. The laundryman.
